speaker: Raquel Urtasun
title: An AI-First Approach to Enable Self Driving at Scale, with Raquel Urtasun of Waabi
question: In traditional modular autonomous driving stacks, why does patching newly observed road errors make engineering development progressively harder to scale?
guest: When you observe a particular error, basically this is categorized in terms of what kind of mistakes we see, and then there is a team that is tasked with solving this type of error. In order to do so, they basically go and build yet another model, one of these small models within hundreds and hundreds of these models that form a very complicated software stack, all with dependencies. This is one of the reasons why this technology doesn't really scale, and why every time you add one of these models, you pay the cost that you need more maintenance, and you need to grow your team even farther. On top of this, you have this complicated expert system, where if this happens in the world, you should behave this way. As a consequence, every time there is a change that you want to make in the software stack, you need to tune every single model one at a time until you end up at the end of the stack. Typically every time you create one of these changes, it takes almost a quarter or more to land it in production, even if it's a very small change.

points.core: Every added model compounds cross-stack dependency maintenance across hundreds of coupled components.
points.note: Accept: growing dependency entanglement, maintenance overhead, or required team headcount each time another module is added to the stack. Do not credit: generic mentions of hiring costs or compute expenses.

points.core: Any stack change requires manually retuning downstream modules sequentially one at a time.
points.note: Accept: serial hand-tuning of every subsequent model or rule-based heuristic down the pipeline whenever an upstream change is made. Do not credit: generic mentions of slow QA or code review.

points.core: Serial manual tuning stretches production release cycles for minor changes to a quarter.
points.note: Accept: months-long or quarter-plus iteration latency to ship even small updates because hand-tuning lacks automation. Do not credit: vague statements that development is slow without tying it to serial tuning.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
In a traditional modular stack (perception → prediction → planning → control), much of the behavior, especially in planning, is encoded as hand-written rules, heuristics, and hand-designed interfaces between modules. When a new failure appears on the road, engineers typically fix it by adding another rule, special case, or tuned parameter aimed at that specific scenario.

This scales poorly for several reasons. The long tail of rare driving situations is effectively unbounded, so the stream of patches never ends. Each new rule interacts with all the existing ones, so the codebase grows more complex and brittle, and a fix for one scenario can cause regressions in others, making validation increasingly expensive. Modules are also developed and optimized separately against their own proxy metrics, so errors compound downstream, and a change in one module can force retuning of the others. Finally, the narrow hand-defined interfaces discard information, so some failures cannot be fixed without redesigning them.

The result is that engineering effort grows with every fix, rather than performance improving mainly through more data and compute, which is the central argument for learned, end-to-end approaches.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: In traditional modular autonomous driving stacks, perception, prediction, planning, and control communicate through hand-designed interfaces, turning edge-case patching into a compounding bottleneck. Because fixed intermediate abstractions like bounding boxes discard rich contextual cues, handling an unforeseen road scenario often requires expanding interface schemas across multiple teams. Within individual modules, engineers typically patch failures by adding bespoke rules, thresholds, or specialized sub-models. As thousands of patches accumulate to address the long tail of rare events, overlapping heuristics interact unpredictably, creating a "whack-a-mole" dynamic where fixing one failure silently regresses previously working behaviors. Moreover, because each module optimizes local proxy metrics rather than a unified driving objective, errors cascade ambiguously across boundaries, and retraining or retuning an upstream component shifts the input distributions that downstream logic implicitly relies upon. Consequently, every new patch increases architectural entanglement, cross-team coordination, and system-wide validation overhead while delivering diminishing gains in overall driving performance.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
In a traditional modular stack, perception, prediction, planning, and control are separate components. They are joined by hand-designed interfaces and governed largely by hand-written rules and heuristics. When a new failure shows up on the road, such as an odd construction zone, an unusual pedestrian behavior, or a strange intersection, engineers usually fix it by adding another rule, threshold, or special case to one module.

Each patch tends to fix only that specific scenario and doesn't generalize. Real-world driving has an effectively endless long tail of edge cases, so the patches pile up without limit. They also interact: a change in perception or planning can quietly break behavior somewhere else, because modules depend on each other's outputs through fixed interfaces that drop information and pass errors downstream. As the rulebase grows, the possible conflicts multiply faster than the rules themselves. Regression testing, validation, and debugging get more expensive with every fix, and the codebase becomes brittle and hard to reason about.

So engineering effort grows faster than capability improves. That is why companies like Wayve and Tesla argue for end-to-end learned systems, where new failures are fixed by adding data instead of code.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
In traditional modular autonomous driving stacks, driving is split into sequential subsystems—such as perception, prediction, planning, and control—connected by hand-engineered interfaces and rule-based heuristics. When engineers patch a newly observed road error by adding a special-case rule, tuning a cost-function weight, or adjusting a perception threshold, the change rarely stays isolated. Because downstream modules depend tightly on upstream outputs and assumptions, fixing one edge case frequently shifts error distributions and triggers regressions in previously working scenarios.

As fleets encounter the virtually unbounded long tail of real-world driving, each new patch adds another layer of interacting heuristics, exceptions, and tunable parameters. Over time, these rules begin to conflict in unpredictable ways, making it increasingly difficult to attribute failures to a single module or anticipate the system-wide impact of any edit. Instead of compounding progress, engineering teams spend a growing share of their effort untangling brittle interactions, retuning coupled parameters, and revalidating the entire stack, causing development complexity to grow faster than driving capability.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
In a traditional modular driving stack, perception, prediction, and planning pass simplified representations to one another. A road error can arise from how those modules interact, so a fix may require tracing the failure across several interfaces. For example, making the planner brake earlier can help when an object is detected late, but it can also cause unnecessary braking when detections are noisy.

As engineers add rules, thresholds, and exceptions, each patch has more existing behavior to interact with. A fix for one scenario can create regressions in others, so engineers have to test each change against a growing set of scenarios. Over time, the work of maintaining and validating the patches grows along with the work of handling new road errors.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A newly observed driving error may involve several modules. For example, late braking can result from a missed detection, an inaccurate prediction of another vehicle’s motion, or a planner that waits too long to react. Engineers have to trace the error across those boundaries before deciding what to change.

A patch that fixes one encounter can also change behavior in situations the car previously handled well. Making the planner brake earlier, for instance, may cause unnecessary braking elsewhere. As rules, thresholds, and exceptions accumulate, each new fix has more interactions to check. Engineers spend progressively more time diagnosing failures, coordinating changes, and testing for regressions, while unfamiliar road situations continue to surface.
